title: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
hookLine: Ruth clings to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"
last: STAY BESIDE THEM, LET THEIR WORDS STAND.

lines: GO BACK, I HAVE NOTHING TO GIVE.
cards: On the road out of Moab, Naomi keeps sending her daughters-in-law home, and her argument is practical, almost brutal. I'm too old to have a husband. Even if I had sons tonight, would you wait for them to grow up?
Go back. Orpah weeps, kisses her, and turns for home, and the book never blames her. Ruth doesn't move.

So Naomi points after her. In the King James: "Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law." It's the last door Naomi can open for her.

teach.h: PAST A LIFETIME, TO THE GRAVE.
teach.b: Ruth's answer holds today's title: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Listen to how it ends.
"Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me." Three things are packed in.
First, she goes past a lifetime: not just I'll come with you, but I'll be buried where you're buried. Not even her bones are going back to Moab.
Second, she seals it with an oath by the LORD, the name of Naomi's God: a woman of Moab, on a road out of Moab, binding herself in the name she's choosing. Third, look at Naomi.
"When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her."

teach.h: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: That's all. No embrace in the text. No thank you.

teach.h: NAOMI SAYS NOTHING, AND THEY WALK ON.
teach.b: Naomi just stops arguing, they walk on, and the next thing she says out loud, at the gate, is that she came home empty. Ruth's loyalty isn't thanked on the spot. It doesn't need to be.

The rabbis heard more. In the Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, they imagine a whole conversation hidden in the speech: Naomi naming, one by one, what this life will ask of her, and each of Ruth's phrases answering, I accept.
And some readers find one word under all of it, a word Ruth never says but lives out: chesed, loyal kindness that keeps going after it's been told to stop.

how: Jews read Ruth's vow in the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and Jewish tradition looks to Ruth as the example of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice.

o: pity felt for a stranger, from a safe distance
a strict duty, paid back only to those who were kind
loyal kindness that keeps going, even when told to stop

games.q: thy people, my people — tap the pairs.

s: Ruth promises to go with Naomi only until Bethlehem
"where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried."
the book blames Orpah for turning back
Orpah weeps, kisses Naomi and goes, and the book never blames her.
Ruth swears her oath by the LORD
"the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me."

games.q: you're Naomi. Ruth has just sworn to live where you live and be buried where you're buried. what do you do?
o: thank her and hold her close.
keep arguing until she goes home.
games.why: "when she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her." no thanks in the text, just silence, and the road.

practice: Bring to mind someone hard to stay with right now, not someone who harms you, but someone grieving, prickly or distant, and walk beside them in your mind on a long road.
Ask what staying would look like: a call you keep making, a seat saved, a message that asks for nothing back. If you pray, you can say their name to God as you walk.

wordCard.voice: chesed, the loyal kindness that keeps going even after it's been told to stop, which Ruth lives out but never names. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: "thy people, my people," two words in Ruth 1:16.

carryVoice: Your line: thy people, my people. Loyalty that doesn't wait for thanks. Day eight hundred thirty-five, done.
